# Evaluating hallucination detection for LLM outputs

![](../images/model-evaluation.svg){.project-hero fig-alt="Illustration of a systematic evaluation and model comparison"}

::: {.project-meta}
**Context:** private Qlik/Talend industrial project  
**Focus:** benchmark design · model evaluation · LLM/NLP  
**Disclosure:** methodology and qualitative comparative observations only
:::

## The question

Language-model outputs can be fluent while containing unsupported claims. The project examined how to compare approaches intended to identify hallucinations or assess factual support, using a benchmark rather than relying on anecdotal examples or a single model judgement.

## Evaluation workflow

::: {.method-grid}
::: {.method-card}
### 1. Research the field
Review the state of the art and define the evaluation scope.
:::
::: {.method-card}
### 2. Build a benchmark
Create an independent pipeline and a common comparison protocol.
:::
::: {.method-card}
### 3. Compare approaches
Use Amazon Bedrock to evaluate an AWS guardrail-based approach against state-of-the-art small language models (SLMs), alongside complementary fact-checking and LLM-evaluation methods.
:::
::: {.method-card}
### 4. Analyse behaviour
Calculate and aggregate metrics, study threshold-dependent trade-offs, inspect errors, and expose results through an interactive Streamlit interface.
:::
:::

## Transferable lesson

Evaluation needs to be interpreted against the chosen metric, operating threshold, dataset, and observed failure patterns. A managed provider feature or a larger model should not be assumed to be better without systematic comparison.

The work covered the research-to-evaluation loop: state-of-the-art review, scoping, integration, metric design, benchmark execution, error analysis, and communication of limitations.

## Confidentiality

Qlik/Talend has not authorised disclosure of aggregate numerical results. This public case study therefore contains no numerical scores, rankings, private repository links, source code, internal datasets, implementation-specific architecture, or other proprietary details. It does not claim that one approach is universally best.
